quarterly_data.signal: LINE-LEVEL CAPACITY UNIT AND UTILIZATION (the ~200,000/month-now to 650,000/month-by-end-2026 path was already given on the Q2 FY2026 earnings call; new here is what one production 'line' is and how hard it runs): CFO/CSO Stefan Murry said AOI plans production in blocks of '100,000 units per month capacity' (what he would call a line), run essentially 24/7 apart from maintenance downtime because the transceiver process is automated. Asked whether AOI is at about 200,000 units now heading to 650,000 by year end, he confirmed: 'Probably a little more than 200,000. We were 200,000 kind of at the end of last quarter', and AOI is 'on that pathway between 200 and 650'.
quarterly_data.figure: 100,000 units per month capacity; Probably a little more than 200,000; on that pathway between 200 and 650

quarterly_data.signal: SOLD OUT AND TURNING CUSTOMERS AWAY: Murry said that when another large data center customer asks for units today AOI has to answer that it is 'sold out at least through second half of next year and beyond'. Some large data center customers have already approached AOI ('some have') and it cannot take them without over-committing against existing customers; the only way in may be CPO or another newer technology further out. He confirmed the monthly data center transceiver target put to him is a REVENUE expectation, not merely a capacity figure, and said AOI could do more revenue than that if it had more capacity - 'the demand is not the limiting factor', capacity and to some extent supply chain are. Best case long-term share is 'somewhere around 20% market share'. Several LTAs are on the table but AOI is deliberately cautious: an LTA that locks up too much capacity for one customer could scare away other customers it wants later.
quarterly_data.figure: sold out at least through second half of next year and beyond; somewhere around 20% market share

quarterly_data.signal: WHERE THE 800G RAMP IS PHYSICALLY COMING FROM: Murry said 'two major hyperscale customers' are both buying meaningful 800G quantities with several smaller customers either buying or about to start. The step up from 'a few million dollars in 800G sales a quarter' to the Q3/Q4 projection comes MAINLY OUT OF THE TAIWAN PLANT - that is the capacity added this year. The Houston/US real estate starts only its very first increment later this year and is really a 2027 and into 2028 contributor.
quarterly_data.figure: two major hyperscale customers; a few million dollars in 800G sales a quarter

quarterly_data.signal: LASER FAB FOOTPRINT AND THE US PREMIUM: Murry said 'the lasers are only made here in the U.S.' in the Sugar Land facility, that AOI intends to add further laser production in the Houston area but does NOT intend to put laser production overseas, and that the added laser capacity lands mostly in the latter half of next year aimed at CPO/NPO devices. Asked whether customers pay up for that, he said flatly they are 'willing to pay a premium for U.S. production' - driven by the non-zero possibility of a ban on Chinese-sourced optics, which customers say would kill their ability to build new US data centers.
quarterly_data.figure: the lasers are only made here in the U.S.; willing to pay a premium for U.S. production

quarterly_data.signal: MEMORY SHORTAGE IS DRIVING THE 100G DECLINE (the Q2 FY2026 call already attributed the 100G weakness to the memory shortage; new here is the customer's allocation mechanism and the expedite-fee timing): Murry explained the unexpected margin headwind as 'one of our customers was unable to secure enough memory to meet all of their build-out needs', so that customer is reallocating the memory it can get to higher-speed nodes (800G, 1.6T) and deploying relatively fewer 100G links for the next few quarters - which hits AOI's high-margin 100G business. On expedite fees, he said the 1.6T volume came up faster than AOI's SUPPLIERS had planned for (they had discounted AOI's forecast and are now tight on capacity), but that this irons itself out over the next few months and should not be much of a factor beyond Q4.
quarterly_data.figure: one of our customers was unable to secure enough memory to meet all of their build-out needs

quarterly_data.signal: CPO PIPELINE AND CPO MARGIN STRUCTURE: Murry said AOI has 'five companies' it is talking to about CPO, some of which are also in real NPO discussions, and expects MORE THAN ONE CPO customer - but probably not all five, because it will not have enough capacity for everyone. On economics, CPO ELSFP or laser-diode margins 'should be meaningfully above 40%', with the bare laser chip 'most likely above 60%' and modules in between, so CPO/NPO mix can pull group margin above the 40% long-term target once it scales.
quarterly_data.figure: five companies; margins should be meaningfully above 40%; most likely above 60%

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE-UP LASER CONTENT - THE INDUSTRY CAPACITY GAP QUANTIFIED: Murry agreed scale-up optics is 'an order of magnitude-ish increase' in the NUMBER of lasers per rack versus scale-out, and added the die itself is 'five or six times larger size per laser', so the wafer real estate the industry must process rises enormously. He said there is not enough capacity in the industry right now to come close to meeting scale-up demand, let alone scale-out - which is why AOI and its competitors are all investing in laser fabs. He called the AI shift in optics the most impactful game changer he has seen in 30 years in the business.
quarterly_data.figure: an order of magnitude-ish increase; five or six times larger size per laser

quarterly_data.signal: WAFER SIZE AND SUBSTRATE SUPPLY: AOI runs lasers on four-inch wafers today; all fab equipment bought in the last year or two can go to six-inch and AOI will switch only when six-inch is cheaper per laser than four-inch and six-inch substrate availability exists - no date is set in stone. On substrates, Murry said AOI feels good about availability through next year, through 2027, and is actively working with a number of vendors to secure 2028-and-beyond capacity; substrate pricing 'has gone up a little bit' but is not a dramatic margin impact, and laser yields still have room to improve, which can offset the higher substrate cost.
quarterly_data.figure: We are a four-inch right now; pricing has gone up a little bit
